title: Auth & Security
intro: Security questions test whether you can be trusted with user data. Interviewers expect you to know how to store passwords, how sessions and tokens really work, and the common web attacks — XSS, CSRF, injection, SSRF, prototype pollution — together with the concrete Node code that prevents them. A senior answer names the threat first, then the defense, then the trade-off or the gap that remains.

questions.title: Hashing passwords
questions.question: How should you store user passwords in a Node application? Why not just SHA-256 them?
questions.short: Never store passwords or reversible encryptions of them. Store a hash from a slow, salted password-hashing function: argon2id is the current first choice, bcrypt (cost 12 or so) or scrypt are fine. A unique random salt per password stops rainbow tables and makes equal passwords hash differently; the cost factor makes each guess expensive. SHA-256 is designed to be fast — GPUs compute billions per second — so a leaked database of SHA-256 hashes is cracked quickly even with salts.
questions.simple: A password hash should be like a lock that takes a full second to try each key. Honest users try once; attackers trying billions of keys are stuck.

explain.p: The threat is a database leak. The attacker has the hashes and can guess offline as fast as their hardware allows. Your job is to make each guess as slow and as memory-hungry as you can afford at login time.

head: Algorithm
Status
Notes
rows: Cost 10–12+. Only the first 72 bytes of the password are used
Needs very high iterations (hundreds of thousands)
Fast by design; salting alone does not save it

explain.caption: bcrypt: use the async API so hashing runs on the libuv thread pool, not the event loop

list: The salt is stored inside the hash string with the parameters. You do not need a separate column.

Use the async functions. A 100–300 ms hash on the main thread blocks every other request. Native argon2/bcrypt and `crypto.scrypt` run on the libuv thread pool (default 4 threads) — at high login rates that pool becomes a bottleneck.
When you raise the cost later, rehash on next successful login (`argon2.needsRehash`, or compare bcrypt rounds).
Return the same error for "no such user" and "wrong password", and avoid timing differences (hash a dummy when the user does not exist) to prevent user enumeration.
A pepper (secret key kept outside the DB, for example HMAC before hashing) adds protection if only the DB leaks.

explain.note: Hashing is not encryption. You can never get the password back, and you should never need to. Password reset works by sending a one-time token, not the password.

followups.q: Why is a unique salt per user needed?
followups.a: Without salts, identical passwords give identical hashes, and attackers can use precomputed tables. With a unique salt each hash must be attacked separately.

followups.q: How do you pick the cost?
followups.a: Tune it so hashing takes roughly 100–500 ms on your production hardware, and check your login throughput. Raise it over time as hardware gets faster.

followups.q: What is the bcrypt 72-byte limit about?
followups.a: bcrypt ignores bytes after the 72nd, so very long passphrases are truncated. argon2 has no such limit. Some apps pre-hash with HMAC-SHA-256 before bcrypt, but this needs care (encode the output, not raw bytes).

mistakes: Using SHA-256 or MD5, with or without salt.
Encrypting passwords so they can be "recovered".
Using hashSync / compareSync in request handlers.
Logging passwords in request bodies or error messages.

questions.title: Sessions vs JWT
questions.question: Compare server-side sessions with JWTs for authenticating users. Which would you choose for a typical web app?
questions.short: With sessions, the server stores session data (in Redis or a DB) and the client only holds a random session id, usually in an httpOnly cookie. Revoking is easy — delete the session — but every request needs a store lookup. A JWT is a signed token that carries the claims itself, so any server with the key can verify it without a lookup, which is handy across services. The cost is that you cannot easily revoke it before it expires. For a typical browser app on one backend, sessions in httpOnly cookies are simpler and safer; JWTs fit API-to-API and multi-service setups, with short expiry plus refresh tokens.
questions.simple: A session is a cloakroom ticket: the number means nothing alone, the cloakroom has your coat. A JWT is a signed pass that carries your details on it — anyone can check the signature, but you cannot cancel it once handed out.

head: Server session
JWT (stateless)
rows: Hard: wait for expiry or keep a denylist

list: "JWTs are more secure" — no. Both are bearer credentials; whoever holds them is you.
"Sessions do not scale" — a Redis lookup is sub-millisecond and scales well.
"JWT means no cookies" — a JWT can be stored in a cookie; storage and token format are separate decisions.
"Stateless JWT with logout" — real logout or ban needs state somewhere (denylist, token version per user, or short expiry with refresh tokens).

explain.note: Whatever you choose: regenerate the session id (or issue new tokens) on login and privilege change, expire sessions after inactivity, and destroy server state on logout.

followups.q: What is session fixation?
followups.a: An attacker gets a victim to use a session id the attacker knows, then waits for them to log in. Regenerating the session id on login makes the old id useless.

followups.q: How do you log a user out of all devices with JWTs?
followups.a: Store a tokenVersion (or 'valid after' timestamp) per user, include it in tokens, and reject tokens with an older value. That is a lookup per request, which is basically a session — or rely on short access tokens and revoke refresh tokens.

followups.q: Where does express-session keep data by default?
followups.a: In a MemoryStore, which leaks memory and is not shared between processes. It is for development only; use Redis or a DB store in production.

mistakes: Using JWTs for a simple single-server web app and then building a denylist that recreates sessions.
Using the default MemoryStore in production.
Not regenerating the session id at login.
Putting sensitive data in a JWT payload, which is only encoded, not encrypted.

questions.title: JWT structure and verification
questions.question: Explain the structure of a JWT. What is the difference between signing and encrypting it, and what must you check when verifying one?
questions.short: A JWT is three base64url parts joined by dots: header (alg, typ, kid), payload (claims like sub, exp, iat, iss, aud) and signature. A normal JWT (JWS) is signed, not encrypted: anyone can decode and read the payload, but nobody can change it without breaking the signature. Encryption is a different format, JWE. To verify: pin the allowed algorithms yourself, check the signature with the right key, then check exp and nbf, and iss and aud. Never trust the header's alg blindly — that is how 'alg: none' and RS256-to-HS256 confusion attacks work.
questions.simple: A JWT is a postcard with a wax seal. Everyone can read the postcard; the seal only proves nobody changed it.

list: HS256 (HMAC): one shared secret signs and verifies. Simple, but every verifier can also mint tokens. Use a long random secret (32+ bytes).
RS256 / ES256 / EdDSA (asymmetric): the auth server signs with a private key; others verify with the public key, often fetched from a JWKS URL and selected by `kid`. Best when many services verify.
JWE: actually encrypts the payload. Rarely needed — usually just keep secrets out of the token.
Allowlist algorithms (`algorithms: ['RS256']`). The token's header is attacker-controlled.
Verify the signature with the key you expect for that issuer.
`exp` (expiry) and `nbf` (not before), with a small clock tolerance.
`iss` (who issued it) and `aud` (who it is for) — so a token for another service is not accepted by yours.
Only then use claims like `sub` and roles. `jwt.decode()` does NOT verify; never use it for auth.
`alg: none`: an unsigned token. Old or misconfigured libraries accepted it.

Algorithm confusion: the server expects RS256 and verifies with the public key. The attacker sends HS256 signed using that public key as the HMAC secret. If the library picks the algorithm from the header, it verifies. Pinning `algorithms` stops it.
Weak HS256 secrets can be brute-forced offline from any captured token.
`kid` or `jku` headers used to load keys from attacker-controlled places.

explain.note: Keep payloads small and non-sensitive: user id, roles/scopes, expiry. They are readable by anyone holding the token, and they ride on every request.

anim.title: What jwt.verify checks, in order

steps.note: The middleware takes the token from "Authorization: Bearer ...".
First check: is the header alg in our allowlist? HS256 is allowed.
Recompute HMAC-SHA256 over header.payload with our secret and compare to the signature. They match.
exp is in the future, so the token has not expired.
iss and aud match what this API expects. The token was made for us.
All checks pass. The decoded claims go on req.user and the request continues.
An attacker edits the payload to role "admin" and sets alg to "none". "none" is not in the allowlist.
verify throws and we answer 401. Without the allowlist, a weak setup might have accepted it.
A valid but old token fails the exp check with TokenExpiredError, also 401. The client should refresh.

followups.q: Is the JWT payload encrypted?
followups.a: No. It is base64url-encoded JSON. Anyone can decode it. Only JWE encrypts, and it is a different format.

followups.q: How do you rotate signing keys?
followups.a: With asymmetric keys and a JWKS: publish the new public key with a new kid, start signing with it, keep the old key in the JWKS until all old tokens expire, then remove it.

followups.q: What library would you use?
followups.a: jsonwebtoken is the classic choice for Node; jose is a modern, dependency-free library that supports JWS, JWE and JWKS fetching and works in other runtimes too. Either way, pass explicit algorithms, issuer and audience.

mistakes: Using jwt.decode() and trusting the result.
Not pinning allowed algorithms.
Putting secrets or personal data in the payload thinking it is encrypted.
Using a short, guessable HS256 secret.

questions.title: Access tokens, refresh tokens, storage
questions.question: How do access and refresh tokens work together? How do you handle rotation and revocation, and where should a browser app store them?
questions.short: The access token is short-lived (5–15 minutes) and sent on every API call; it is usually a JWT verified without a DB lookup. The refresh token is long-lived, random, stored hashed on the server, and only sent to the refresh endpoint to get new tokens. With rotation, every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one; if an old one is ever reused, assume theft and revoke the whole token family. In the browser, keep the refresh token in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie scoped to the refresh path, and the access token in memory — not localStorage, which any XSS can read.
questions.simple: The access token is a day pass that expires fast. The refresh token is the membership card kept in a locked drawer, used only to print new day passes, and replaced each time it is used.

explain.p: Short access tokens limit the damage if one leaks, without forcing users to log in every 10 minutes. The refresh token is checked against the server, so that is where you get revocation: logout, password change or 'sign out everywhere' deletes the refresh tokens, and access dies within minutes.

head: Where
XSS can steal it?
CSRF risk?
Notes
rows: Any injected script reads it. Avoid for long-lived tokens
Lost on reload; refresh on load via cookie
Yes, mitigate with SameSite + CSRF token
Best for refresh tokens and sessions

list: Store only a hash (for example SHA-256) of each refresh token, with userId, familyId, expiresAt, usedAt.
On refresh: look it up, check expiry, mark it used, issue a new one in the same family.
If a used token comes back, someone has a copy. Revoke the family: both the attacker and the user must log in again.
Allow a tiny grace period for legitimate races (two tabs refreshing at once), or serialize refreshes on the client.

explain.note: httpOnly does not make XSS harmless — injected script can still call your API from the page while the user is there. It just stops the token from being stolen and used elsewhere for 30 days. XSS prevention still matters most.

anim.title: Login, refresh with rotation, and a stolen token

steps.note: User logs in with email and password. The API checks the password hash.
A random refresh token rt1 is created. Only its hash is stored, in a new family F1.
rt1 goes in an httpOnly cookie. A 10-minute access JWT goes in the JSON body; the app keeps it in memory.
API calls send "Authorization: Bearer access#1". No DB lookup needed until it expires.
Ten minutes later the access token expires. The app calls /auth/refresh; the browser attaches rt1.
rt1 is valid and unused. Mark it used, then issue rt2 in the same family.
The browser gets the new cookie rt2 and a fresh access token. rt1 is now worthless.
An attacker who copied rt1 earlier tries to use it. It is marked used: that should never happen.
Reuse means theft. Revoke the whole family F1, including the user's current rt2.
The real user's next refresh fails too, so they log in again. The attacker is locked out; access#2 dies within 10 minutes.

followups.q: Why store refresh tokens hashed?
followups.a: If the DB leaks, attackers cannot use the stored values. Refresh tokens are long random strings, so a fast hash like SHA-256 is enough (no need for bcrypt).

followups.q: How do you revoke an access token immediately?
followups.a: You mostly cannot without state. Options: keep access tokens very short, keep a denylist of jti values until their exp, or check a per-user token version on each request.

followups.q: What is the BFF pattern?
followups.a: Backend-for-frontend: a server-side component holds the tokens and the browser only has a session cookie to that server. Tokens never reach browser JS at all, which is the recommended approach for sensitive apps.

mistakes: Long-lived access tokens (days) with no refresh flow or revocation.
Storing refresh tokens in localStorage.
Not rotating refresh tokens, or rotating without reuse detection.
Storing refresh tokens in plain text in the database.

questions.title: OAuth2 / OIDC login with PKCE
questions.question: You need "Sign in with Google" (or any OIDC provider). Walk through the authorization code flow with PKCE from the Node backend's point of view.
questions.short: The backend redirects the browser to the provider's authorize endpoint with client_id, redirect_uri, scope 'openid', a random state, a nonce, and a PKCE code_challenge — the SHA-256 of a secret code_verifier it keeps in the session. After login the provider redirects back with a one-time code and the state. The backend checks state, then exchanges the code plus code_verifier (and client secret if it has one) at the token endpoint over a back channel. It verifies the ID token — signature via JWKS, iss, aud, exp, nonce — then finds or creates the user by issuer + sub and starts its own session.
questions.simple: It is like a hotel checking your passport through the embassy. You go to the embassy, they give you a one-time slip, and the hotel calls the embassy directly with that slip plus a secret only the hotel knows.

list: OAuth2 is about authorization: getting an access token to call an API on the user's behalf.
OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds authentication on top: an ID token (a JWT) that says who the user is (`sub`, `email`, ...). "Sign in with X" is OIDC.

head: Value
Protects against
rows: CSRF on the callback: an attacker cannot make you finish their login flow
A stolen authorization code is useless without the verifier
Replay of an old ID token into a new login
Codes being sent to an attacker-controlled URL
Tokens never pass through the browser URL

list: Use a certified library such as `openid-client` instead of hand-rolling token validation. It handles discovery (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`), JWKS caching and the checks.
Identify users by `iss` + `sub`, not by email. Emails can change and, depending on the provider, may not be verified (`email_verified`).
After the callback, create your own session (cookie) — you usually do not need to keep the provider's tokens unless you call their APIs.
PKCE is now recommended for every client, including confidential server-side ones (OAuth 2.1 direction). The implicit flow is deprecated.

explain.note: Keep the state, verifier and nonce in a server-side session or a short-lived, signed, httpOnly cookie — never in localStorage — and delete them after the callback so they cannot be reused.

anim.title: Authorization code + PKCE, step by step

steps.note: The user clicks "Sign in". The browser calls GET /login on your backend.
Create a random code_verifier and its SHA-256 hash, the code_challenge. Only the hash will be sent out.
Save verifier, state and nonce in the server-side session for this browser.
Redirect the browser to the provider with client_id, redirect_uri, state, nonce and the challenge.
The user logs in and consents on the provider's page. The provider remembers the challenge with a new one-time code.
The provider redirects back to /callback?code=XY7&state=a81f. state matches, so this is the flow we started.
Server-to-server POST: code + verifier (+ client secret). The provider hashes the verifier and compares it to the stored challenge.
The provider returns an ID token. Verify signature via JWKS, iss, aud = our client_id, exp, and nonce = 7cd2.
Find or create the local user by iss + sub, regenerate the session id, store userId.
Redirect to the app. From now on the browser just uses your normal session cookie.

followups.q: Why is PKCE needed if the backend has a client secret?
followups.a: It protects against authorization code injection and interception: even if a code leaks via logs, browser history or a malicious app, it cannot be redeemed without the verifier. Current best practice recommends PKCE for all clients.

followups.q: What is the difference between the ID token and the access token?
followups.a: The ID token is for your app: it tells you who logged in. The access token is for calling an API (the resource server). Do not send ID tokens to APIs as access tokens, and do not use access tokens to identify users in your app.

followups.q: How would your API validate access tokens from an external provider?
followups.a: Fetch and cache the provider's JWKS, verify the JWT signature with the key matching kid, and check iss, aud (your API), exp and required scopes. Libraries like jose (createRemoteJWKSet) handle this.

mistakes: Skipping the state check on the callback.
Linking accounts by email without checking email_verified or the issuer.
Decoding the ID token without verifying it.
Putting tokens in the redirect URL or in localStorage.

questions.title: CORS: what it protects
questions.question: What does CORS actually protect against, and what does it not protect against?
questions.short: The browser's same-origin policy stops a page from reading responses from other origins. CORS is the server's way to relax that rule for specific origins with Access-Control-Allow-* headers. It protects users: evil.com cannot use the victim's logged-in browser to read data from your API. It is not server-side access control — curl ignores it — and it does not stop simple cross-site requests from being sent, so it is not CSRF protection. A preflight OPTIONS is sent for non-simple requests, which does block those from being sent when not allowed.
questions.simple: CORS is the browser asking your API, "May this other website read your answer?" It is a rule for browsers, not a lock on your server.

explain.p: Scheme + host + port. `https://app.example.com` and `https://api.example.com` are different origins. So are `http://` and `https://`, and port 3000 vs 3001.

list: Without CORS restrictions, any site the user visits could `fetch` your API with the user's cookies and read the response: their profile, their messages.
With a strict allowlist, only your own frontends can read responses in the browser.
Non-browser clients: scripts, curl, other servers ignore CORS. Authenticate and authorize every request on the server.
Simple requests (form POST, GET with no custom headers) are still sent. The server executes them; only reading the response is blocked. A state-changing simple request is a CSRF risk.
Data your API returns to an allowed origin that is compromised (XSS on your own frontend).

explain.note: Do not allow the `null` origin. Sandboxed iframes and some redirects send `Origin: null`, and an attacker can produce it easily.

followups.q: What makes a request trigger a preflight?
followups.a: A method other than GET/HEAD/POST, custom headers like Authorization or X-Requested-With, or a Content-Type other than form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain (application/json triggers it).

followups.q: Why does Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * not work with cookies?
followups.a: The spec forbids wildcard with credentials. The server must echo a specific origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

followups.q: Can a server-side CORS check stop scraping?
followups.a: No. Anyone can send requests without an Origin header or with a fake one from outside a browser. Use authentication and rate limiting.

mistakes: Treating CORS as API authentication.
Using origin: true or a loose regex with credentials.
Assuming CORS blocks a cross-site request from being sent at all.

questions.title: CSRF and SameSite cookies
questions.question: What is CSRF, and how do SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens protect against it?
questions.short: CSRF is when a malicious site makes the user's browser send a request to your site, and the browser automatically attaches your cookies, so the request runs as the logged-in user. It only matters for cookie-based (ambient) auth. SameSite=Lax or Strict stops cookies from being sent on cross-site subrequests and POSTs; Lax still sends them on top-level GET navigations, so GETs must never change state. Add defense in depth for sensitive actions: a CSRF token (synchronizer or double-submit), or checking Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site headers. Bearer tokens in an Authorization header are not sent automatically, so they are not exposed to CSRF.
questions.simple: Your browser is like a friend who carries your house key everywhere. CSRF tricks that friend into opening your door for a stranger. SameSite tells your friend: only use my key when I sent you myself.

head: Value
Cross-site requests send the cookie?
Notes
rows: Even clicking a link from another site arrives logged out
Default in modern Chrome/Edge when unset. Good baseline
Needed for third-party embeds; full CSRF exposure

explain.p: "Site" means registrable domain (eTLD+1): `app.example.com` and `api.example.com` are the same site, so SameSite does not protect you from a compromised or attacker-controlled sibling subdomain.

list: Synchronizer token: the server stores a random token in the session, renders it into forms or sends it to the SPA, and requires it in a header or field on every unsafe request. evil.example cannot read it.
Double-submit cookie: a random token is in a (non-httpOnly) cookie and must be echoed in a header; preferably signed and bound to the session, because a sibling subdomain can set cookies.
Origin check: for unsafe methods, reject requests whose `Origin` (or `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`) is not yours. Cheap and effective as an extra layer.

explain.caption: Origin / Fetch Metadata check as an extra layer next to SameSite and tokens

explain.note: The old `csurf` package is deprecated. Use a maintained library (for example csrf-csrf for double-submit) or implement the synchronizer pattern with your session store.

anim.title: A forged form POST with and without SameSite

steps.note: The user logs in to bank.example. The browser stores the session cookie. First, imagine it was set with SameSite=None.
Later the user visits evil.example. Its script submits a hidden form to bank.example/transfer.
With SameSite=None, the browser attaches sid to this cross-site POST. The bank sees a valid session.
The transfer runs as the user. CORS does not help: a form POST is a simple request and is sent anyway.
Now the cookie is set with SameSite=Lax, as in the code.
evil.example submits the same form.
It is a cross-site POST, so the browser leaves the cookie out. The bank sees no session and returns 401.
Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET links from other sites. So GET must never change state, and sensitive actions should also check a CSRF token or Origin.

followups.q: Are APIs using Authorization: Bearer headers vulnerable to CSRF?
followups.a: Not to classic CSRF, because the browser does not attach that header automatically. If the token is stored in a cookie and read by the server from the cookie, it is cookie auth again and CSRF applies.

followups.q: Does SameSite=Lax fully replace CSRF tokens?
followups.a: It removes most risk, but not all: state-changing GETs, same-site attacks from sibling subdomains, and older browsers. For high-value actions keep a token or Origin check too.

followups.q: What is login CSRF?
followups.a: The attacker logs the victim into the attacker's account, so the victim's later actions (like saving a card) land in the attacker's account. Protect the login form with a CSRF token or Origin check too.

mistakes: Thinking CORS prevents CSRF.
Changing state on GET requests.
Setting SameSite=None on session cookies without needing it.
Assuming JSON APIs cannot be hit by CSRF (text/plain form tricks and misconfigured parsers can).

questions.title: XSS, output encoding and Helmet
questions.question: What is XSS, how do you prevent it in a Node app, and what do security headers like those set by Helmet add?
questions.short: XSS is when attacker-controlled data ends up executed as script in your page, so it runs with the user's session: it can read the page, call your API and steal tokens kept in JS-accessible storage. The main defense is context-aware output encoding: let templating engines or React escape by default, never inject untrusted HTML, and sanitize with a library like DOMPurify if you must allow rich HTML. Headers are a second layer: a strict Content-Security-Policy blocks inline and foreign scripts; Helmet sets CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, frame protections and more with sane defaults.
questions.simple: XSS is someone slipping a fake instruction into a note your page reads aloud. Encoding means you always read user text as text, never as instructions.

list: Stored: payload saved in your DB (a comment) and shown to other users.
Reflected: payload in the URL echoed back in the response.
DOM-based: frontend JS writes URL data into the DOM (`innerHTML`, `location.hash`).
HTML body: escape `& < > " '`. EJS `<%= %>`, Handlebars `{{ }}`, Pug `#{}` and React JSX do this by default. Their raw forms (`<%- %>`, `{{{ }}}`, `!{}`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`) do not.
Attributes: always quote them, and never put user input into `on*` handlers or `href` without allowing only `http:`/`https:` URLs (`javascript:` URLs run code).
Inside `<script>`: do not build JS with user data. Pass data as JSON in a data attribute, or serialize with a safe serializer that escapes `<` (for example `serialize-javascript`).
For JSON APIs, set `Content-Type: application/json` (Express does) and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` so browsers never treat it as HTML.

head: Header
What it does
rows: Allowlist for scripts, styles, frames, etc. Blocks most injected scripts
Stops browsers guessing content types (e.g. treating text as script)
Limits URL leakage to other sites
Isolates your window from cross-origin popups

explain.note: Helmet's defaults are a good start, but CSP needs tuning for your frontend. Roll it out with `reportOnly: true` first and watch reports, or you will break your own pages.

followups.q: Should you sanitize input or encode output?
followups.a: Encode output, always, in the right context. Input validation helps (reject what you do not expect), but the same data may go into HTML, SQL and logs, and each needs different handling at the point of use.

followups.q: Does an httpOnly cookie stop XSS?
followups.a: It stops the cookie being read by script, but injected script can still perform actions as the user from the page. It limits the damage; it does not prevent XSS.

followups.q: What is a CSP nonce?
followups.a: A random value generated per response, put in the CSP header (script-src 'nonce-abc') and on your legitimate <script nonce="abc"> tags. Injected scripts do not know the nonce, so they are blocked even if inline.

mistakes: Using raw/unescaped template output for user data.
Building HTML strings with template literals in route handlers.
Allowing javascript: URLs in user-supplied links.
Adding Helmet and assuming XSS is solved.

questions.title: Injection and input validation
questions.question: Besides SQL injection, what other injection attacks should a Node developer guard against, and how does input validation fit in?
questions.short: Any time user input is mixed into something that gets interpreted, it can change its meaning. In MongoDB, JSON bodies can contain operators: { "password": { "$ne": null } } turns a lookup into 'any password'. In shell commands, exec with a string runs through a shell, so ; or && run extra commands — use execFile or spawn with an argument array and no shell. Defend at two levels: validate input strictly at the edge (types, formats, lengths, allowlists) so an object never arrives where a string is expected, and use safe APIs at the point of use (parameters, argument arrays, no eval).
questions.simple: Injection is when a user's answer gets read as part of the question. Validation checks the answer is the right kind of thing; safe APIs keep answers and questions in separate boxes.

explain.p: Also beware `$where` and `$function`, which run JavaScript on the server, and query strings: Express's default query parser turns `?age[$gt]=0` into an object. Express 5 uses the simple parser by default, which avoids nested objects, but validation is still the real fix.

list: Prefer `execFile`/`spawn` with an args array. Avoid `shell: true`.
Use `--` where the tool supports it (or pass absolute paths you built) so a filename like `-rf` is not read as an option.
Even better, use a library (for example an image library) instead of shelling out.
`eval`, `new Function`, `vm` with user input: remote code execution. `vm` is not a security sandbox.
Path traversal: `path.join(UPLOADS, req.params.name)` with `../../etc/passwd`. Resolve the path and check it still starts with the base directory.
Header injection / log injection: strip CR/LF from values written to headers or plain-text logs (structured JSON logs help).
Regex DoS (ReDoS): user input against a regex with nested quantifiers can block the event loop. Avoid building regexes from input; limit input length.
Validate on the server, always — client checks are UX only.
Allowlist (what is allowed) beats denylist (what is forbidden).
Check type, length, range and format; reject unknown fields.
Validate early, at the boundary, and work with the parsed result afterwards.

followups.q: How do you safely serve a file by name from a directory?
followups.a: Resolve with path.resolve(base, name), then check the result starts with base + path.sep. Better: store files under generated ids and look up the name in the DB.

followups.q: Is JSON.parse dangerous?
followups.a: Not for code execution, but its output can contain __proto__ keys (prototype pollution when merged) and huge nested structures. Limit body size and validate the shape.

followups.q: What about template injection?
followups.a: If user input is used as a template (not as data passed into a template), template engines can execute code. Never compile templates from user input.

mistakes: Passing req.body fields directly into MongoDB filters.
Using exec with string interpolation.
Thinking validation alone replaces safe APIs at the point of use.
Using vm to run untrusted code believing it is sandboxed.

questions.title: Prototype pollution
questions.question: What is prototype pollution, how does it happen in Node apps, and how do you prevent it?
questions.short: Prototype pollution is when attacker input adds or changes properties on Object.prototype, so every plain object in the process suddenly 'has' them. It typically happens in deep merge, clone or set-by-path code that copies user-controlled keys: JSON.parse creates a real own key named __proto__, and assigning target['__proto__'] reaches the shared prototype. Effects range from logic bypasses (isAdmin is true for everyone) to crashes and even RCE through gadgets in libraries. Prevent it by blocking __proto__, constructor and prototype keys, using Map or Object.create(null) for dictionaries, validating input shapes, and keeping merge libraries patched.
questions.simple: Every object inherits from one shared parent. If an attacker can write on the parent, every child suddenly has that trait too.

explain.p: `{"__proto__": {...}}` in an object literal sets the prototype, but `JSON.parse` creates an ordinary own property named `__proto__`. So `Object.keys(body)` includes it, and a naive merge then evaluates `target['__proto__']`, which is `Object.prototype` itself.

list: Deep merge / extend / clone helpers (old versions of lodash `merge`/`defaultsDeep`, jQuery extend, many small packages).
Set-by-path utilities: `set(obj, req.body.path, value)` with path `__proto__.isAdmin` or `constructor.prototype.isAdmin`.
Query-string parsers that create nested objects (`?__proto__[isAdmin]=1`). The `qs` library blocks this by default now, but custom parsers may not.
Skip dangerous keys (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `prototype`) in any code that copies keys from input.
Validate input with a strict schema; unknown keys are rejected or stripped.
Use `Map` for user-keyed dictionaries, or `Object.create(null)` objects that have no prototype.
Check own properties with `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` instead of `obj[key]` or `in` when reading options.
Node flags: `--disable-proto=delete` removes the `__proto__` accessor; `Object.freeze(Object.prototype)` at startup makes pollution fail (test carefully; some libraries break).
Keep dependencies updated; `npm audit` catches many known pollution bugs.

explain.note: Pollution is process-wide and persists until restart. One request can change behavior for every later request, which makes it hard to debug.

anim.title: One JSON body poisons every object

steps.note: JSON.parse creates a normal object with an own key literally named "__proto__".
merge loops over own keys of body. The only key is "__proto__", and its value is an object.
target["__proto__"] on a plain {} returns Object.prototype — truthy, so no new object is created.
merge recurses with Object.prototype as the target. That is the shared parent of every object.
It assigns isAdmin = true directly on Object.prototype. The process is now polluted.
A brand-new empty object inherits isAdmin. An "if (user.isAdmin)" check would now pass.
Clean up for the demo: delete the polluted property.
safeMerge skips "__proto__", "constructor" and "prototype" keys, so the payload is ignored.
Object.prototype stays clean, so a fresh object has no isAdmin.

followups.q: How can prototype pollution lead to remote code execution?
followups.a: Through gadgets: library code that reads an option from a plain object without checking own properties. For example, if code builds child_process options from {} and a polluted shell or env property is inherited, an attacker may control the command run.

followups.q: Why does Object.create(null) help?
followups.a: It creates an object with no prototype, so there is no __proto__ accessor and no inherited properties. Writing obj['__proto__'] just creates a normal key.

followups.q: Is structuredClone safe?
followups.a: structuredClone copies own data properties into new plain objects and does not walk into Object.prototype via a __proto__ key, so it is not a pollution vector itself. The risk is in your own merge/set code.

mistakes: Writing a custom deep merge without key filtering.
Assuming JSON.parse output is safe to merge into config objects.
Using plain objects as dictionaries keyed by user input.
Ignoring npm audit warnings for lodash-style merge utilities.

questions.title: Rate limiting and brute-force protection
questions.question: How would you add rate limiting to a Node API and protect the login endpoint from brute-force attacks?
questions.short: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client (by IP, user id or API key) can make in a time window, returning 429 with Retry-After when exceeded. Common algorithms are fixed window, sliding window and token bucket, which allows short bursts up to the bucket size and a steady refill rate. With more than one Node process the counters must live in a shared store like Redis, often via express-rate-limit or rate-limiter-flexible. For login, limit both per IP and per account, add increasing delays or temporary lockouts, and use generic error messages — and remember that enforcing at the proxy or gateway is cheaper than in Node.
questions.simple: Each client gets a bucket of tokens. Every request uses one. Tokens drip back in slowly. Empty bucket means wait.

head: Algorithm
How it works
Trade-off
rows: Count per clock minute, reset at :00
Simple; allows 2x burst around the boundary
Count over the last N seconds
Bucket of size B refills at R/sec; each request takes 1
Protects slow endpoints rather than rate

list: Limit per IP and per username/email. Attackers rotate IPs (credential stuffing) or spread guesses over many accounts.
Prefer progressive delays or temporary lockouts over permanent lockouts, which let attackers lock out real users.
Same response and similar timing for unknown user vs wrong password.
Add CAPTCHA or step-up after suspicious patterns, support MFA, and check passwords against breached lists on sign-up.
Rate limit password reset and OTP endpoints too — 6-digit codes fall quickly without limits.

explain.note: `trust proxy` must match your setup. Too permissive and clients spoof X-Forwarded-For to get a fresh limit per request; not set and every user shares the load balancer's IP.

anim.title: A token bucket: capacity 3, refill 1 per second

steps.note: The bucket starts full: 3 tokens. It refills at 1 token per second, never above 3.
t=0: a request takes one token. Allowed.
t=0: a burst — two more requests take the last two tokens. Bursts up to the capacity are fine.
t=0: a fourth request finds the bucket empty. No time passed, so nothing refilled. 429.
t=1: one second passed, so 1 token was added (elapsed × rate).
That token is taken. Allowed.
Another request at t=1: bucket empty again, so 429. The steady rate is 1 per second.
t=3.5: 2.5 seconds passed, so 2.5 tokens refill (still under the cap of 3).
One token is taken, leaving 1.5. Allowed. In production the state lives in Redis, keyed by IP or user.

followups.q: Why not keep rate limit counters in memory?
followups.a: Each process would have its own counters, so with 8 instances a client gets 8x the limit, and restarts reset everything. A shared store like Redis gives one consistent count.

followups.q: How do you make a Redis-based limiter atomic?
followups.a: Use a single atomic operation such as INCR with EXPIRE in a MULTI, or a Lua script for token bucket math, so concurrent requests cannot both read the old count. Libraries like rate-limiter-flexible do this.

followups.q: Where should rate limiting live?
followups.a: As early as possible: CDN/WAF or API gateway for coarse IP limits, then the app for limits that need user identity or business context, like per-account login attempts.

mistakes: In-memory limits on a multi-instance deployment.
Misconfigured trust proxy, so all users share one IP or attackers spoof it.
Only limiting by IP on login, ignoring per-account attacks.
Forgetting Retry-After so clients retry immediately.

questions.title: Secrets and dependency risks
questions.question: How do you manage secrets in a Node service, and how do you reduce the risk from npm dependencies?
questions.short: Secrets never go in the repo or the Docker image. Inject them at runtime from a secret manager or the platform (Kubernetes secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) as environment variables or mounted files, validate them at startup, and never log them. Use a .env file only in development (Node 20.6+ can load it with --env-file). For dependencies: commit the lockfile and install with npm ci, keep the dependency tree small, run npm audit and automated update PRs, review new packages before adding them, and consider disabling install scripts — supply-chain attacks via typosquatting or compromised maintainers are real.
questions.simple: Keep keys out of the code, like you would not tape your house key to the front door. And be careful who you let into your house — every npm package runs with your app's full permissions.

list: Scan commits for secrets (pre-commit hooks, GitHub secret scanning). If a secret is ever committed, rotate it — deleting the commit is not enough.
Redact secrets in logs (pino `redact`), error reports and crash dumps. Never log `process.env` or full config.
Use different secrets per environment, least privilege for DB users and cloud credentials, and plan for rotation (support two valid keys during a switch).

Environment variables are visible to the whole process and child processes, and sometimes appear in debugging output. For very sensitive values, mounted files or fetching from a secret manager at startup are options.
Commit `package-lock.json` and use `npm ci` in CI and Docker builds for reproducible installs.
`npm audit` (and tools like Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk, Socket) for known vulnerabilities and suspicious packages. Triage: is the vulnerable code path reachable?
Install scripts (`preinstall`, `postinstall`) run arbitrary code at install time. `npm ci --ignore-scripts` reduces that risk (some native packages then need explicit rebuilds).
Check a new package before adding it: maintainers, downloads, recent ownership changes, what it pulls in. Watch for typosquats (`expresss`, `cross-env.js`).
Pin and review updates for critical packages; do not auto-merge major versions blindly.
Run the app as a non-root user in a minimal image so a compromised dependency has less reach.

explain.note: Node 22 includes a permission model (`--permission`, with `--allow-fs-read`, `--allow-fs-write`, `--allow-child-process`, etc.) that can restrict what the process may do. It is a useful extra layer, not a sandbox for untrusted code.

followups.q: Is process.env slow to read?
followups.a: Reading process.env goes through a native lookup each time, so read it once at startup into a config object. That also gives you validation and one place to see all settings.

followups.q: What do you do when npm audit reports a critical vulnerability?
followups.a: Check whether the vulnerable function is used and reachable, upgrade the direct dependency or use npm overrides to force a patched transitive version, and run tests. Document if you accept the risk.

followups.q: Should .env files be used in production?
followups.a: Generally no. Use the platform's secret injection. A .env on a server is an unencrypted file that is easy to leak in backups or images.

mistakes: Committing .env files or baking secrets into Docker images.
Logging the whole config or request headers with tokens.
Using npm install in CI, which can update the lockfile.
Adding packages for trivial tasks without checking them.

questions.title: SSRF basics
questions.question: Your API fetches a URL provided by the user (avatar from URL, webhook, link preview). What is SSRF and how do you defend against it?
questions.short: Server-side request forgery is when an attacker makes your server send requests to places they cannot reach themselves: internal services, localhost admin ports, or the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254 that can hand out credentials. Defend by allowlisting destinations where possible, allowing only http(s), resolving the hostname and rejecting private, loopback and link-local IPs, disabling or re-checking redirects, and setting timeouts and size limits. Network-level egress rules are the strongest layer, and DNS rebinding means you should check the IP you actually connect to, not just a lookup before it.
questions.simple: SSRF is tricking the office assistant into opening internal doors for you. The assistant must check every address against a list before walking anywhere.

list: Cloud metadata endpoints (`http://169.254.169.254/...`) can return IAM credentials. AWS IMDSv2 requires a session token, which helps, but do not rely on it alone.
Internal services often have no auth because they trust the network: admin panels, Redis, Elasticsearch, internal APIs.
Port scanning: the attacker learns your internal network from response times and errors.
Avoid it: if users only pick from known integrations, store ids, not URLs.
Allowlist hosts or domains when the set is known.
Egress firewall / network policy: the service that fetches user URLs cannot reach internal ranges at all. Run it in an isolated network if possible.
In code: parse with `new URL`, allow only `https:` (maybe `http:`), resolve DNS and reject non-public ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16, ::1, fc00::/7, IPv4-mapped IPv6).
Redirects: use `redirect: "error"` or `"manual"` and validate every hop, otherwise a public URL redirects to an internal one.
Timeouts and max response size, so the endpoint cannot be used to tie up your server.

explain.p: The check above resolves the name, then `fetch` resolves it again. An attacker's DNS can answer with a public IP the first time and `127.0.0.1` the second. To close the gap, connect to the exact IP you validated — for example with an undici `Agent` whose `connect.lookup` validates each resolved address — or enforce the rule at the network layer.

explain.note: Do not try to block internal addresses with string checks on the URL. `http://2130706433/`, `http://0x7f.1/`, `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/` and `localhost.attacker.com` all bypass naive filters. Always check the resolved IP.

anim.title: Checking user-supplied URLs before fetching

steps.note: A legitimate avatar URL arrives. new URL() parses it; invalid URLs throw here.
Protocol is https and the host is in the allowlist.
DNS resolves to a public address, so range() is "unicast". Safe to fetch.
fetch runs with redirects disabled and a 5 s timeout.
Attacker sends http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ to grab cloud credentials. Not https: rejected.
Attacker tries https://internal-admin.local/. The host is not on the allowlist.
Suppose an allowed hostname gets a DNS record pointing to 10.0.0.5. The IP check catches the private range.
redirect: "error" stops a public URL from bouncing to an internal one. Remaining gap: DNS rebinding between lookup and connect.

followups.q: Why is fetching user URLs for webhooks risky even with allowlists?
followups.a: Webhook URLs are usually arbitrary customer endpoints, so you cannot allowlist them. That is exactly where IP-range checks, pinned connections, egress isolation and redirect checks matter most.

followups.q: Does blind SSRF matter if you never return the response?
followups.a: Yes. The attacker can still trigger actions on internal services (GET endpoints with side effects), scan ports by timing, and exfiltrate data through DNS.

followups.q: Why use ipaddr.process instead of parse?
followups.a: process converts IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses like ::ffff:10.0.0.5 into IPv4, so the range check sees 'private' instead of 'ipv4Mapped'.

mistakes: Blocking "localhost" and "127.0.0.1" by string match only.
Validating the first URL but following redirects automatically.
Checking DNS once and then letting fetch resolve again.
Forgetting timeouts and size limits on outbound requests.
